documents.title: No uniform Dirichlet floor: λ<sub>min</sub>(G)/mass decays for every window tried
header: > So: does a Dirichlet polynomial of length N have to be large somewhere on the zeros? λ<sub>min</sub>(G)/mass is exactly that question, and the answer is that it decays, for every window tried.

> For the searched-0.12 window the floor runs 0.5685 at N = 8 to 0.0034 at N = 96. Only the Δ = 0.06 window is even a power law: forced through one it gives N<sup>−0.63</sup> with every point within 0.17 in ln. The 0.12 window is not — forced through a power its exponent reads −1.76 and the worst point is 1.52 out in ln, because the decay accelerates. And the gentler window collapses too, just later: 0.040 at N = 128 and 8.6×10⁻³ at N = 160.
> There is no uniform Dirichlet floor here. Changing the sampling did not buy one, and it is worth being plain that this was the outcome hoped for when the section was written.

documents.title: The floor has a scale: a displacement of 0.006 in log doubles it
header: > rh34 §6 found the multiplicative sampling worse conditioned than the lattice and blamed bunching, on one number. (a) asked for that priced. Slide the integers' log-positions linearly towards equispaced over the same range, so that nothing changes but the spacing.

> At the integers λ<sub>min</sub>(G)/mass is 0.2939. At θ = 10<sup>−4</sup> it is 0.2938 — unchanged, so this is not a discontinuity, and the *exactness* of the integers' multiplicative relations is not the mechanism. At θ = 10<sup>−2</sup> it has doubled, to 0.589, while the positions have moved by 0.006 in log and the smallest gap has gone from 0.04256 to 0.04352. Past 5% the curve saturates, wobbling inside a factor 1.06 rather than climbing.
> So the effect has a scale — about 0.006 in log, a seventh of the smallest gap — and the next question is whether any simple statistic is sensitive at it.

documents.title: None of the three statistics predicts the floor; two die by counterexample
documents.raw_status: ** VERIFIED (numerical, five gear sets at N = 24); REFUTED (minimum log-gap and coincidence count as predictors)
header: **Status:** VERIFIED (numerical, five gear sets at N = 24); REFUTED (minimum log-gap and coincidence count as predictors)
> Five gear sets at matched dimension N = 24 say no.

> The **primes** have the smallest minimum log-gap of the five, 0.0278, and the *highest* floor, 0.790; the integers sit at a gap half again as wide and a floor a third the size. Correlation over the five: +0.36 — too weak to carry a story and pointing the wrong way for this one. The **coincidence count** fares no better: the geometric set has the *fewest* distinct log-differences of all, 0.08 of N², and the highest floor; the primes have the *most*, 0.96, and a high floor too; the integers sit in the middle at 0.62 with the lowest floor of the five (−0.15). Reach does not order it either (−0.20).

> (a) therefore closes in the branch rh34 explicitly allowed for. None of the three predicts the floor; two are refuted outright. What replaces them is not an explanation but a measurement: a displacement of 0.006 in log, invisible to every statistic tried, is worth a factor two.

documents.title: The threshold is not a scale but a level crossing
header: > The floor doubles from 0.2939 to 0.5893, as rh35 reported. But nothing deforms into anything. Hold the θ = 0 minimiser fixed and push it through the slide and its own Rayleigh quotient climbs monotonically from 0.2939 to 0.9888: the vector that carried the floor is not made a little dearer, it is destroyed. The floor that replaces it is a *different* vector — the two minimisers overlap 0.088, near enough orthogonal — and the height it lands at was already sitting in the matrix at θ = 0 as the second eigenvalue, 0.5727 against the 0.5893 it arrives at, 2.9%.

> So there is no length scale to find. There is a level that climbs, a level that does not, and an avoided crossing between them at θ = 0.007 where they pass within 0.0426. The "threshold" is where the climbing level overtakes the stationary one, and its height is read off the unperturbed spectrum.

documents.title: Beurling's majorant B: the functional equation B(z) + B(−z) = 2K(z) and a pole-free evaluation
documents.raw_status: ** VERIFIED (numerical; functional equation to 5.6×10⁻¹⁷, B ≥ sgn to −1.7×10⁻¹³ over 400,000 samples)
header: **Status:** VERIFIED (numerical; functional equation to 5.6×10⁻¹⁷, B ≥ sgn to −1.7×10⁻¹³ over 400,000 samples)

> Beurling's function B is the extremal majorant of the sign function: entire of exponential type 2π, B(x) ≥ sgn(x) everywhere, meeting sgn at every nonzero integer, with ∫(B − sgn) = 1 and no majorant of that type doing better.

> Two things had to be got right that recollection got wrong, and both were caught by measuring rather than citing. **B is B alone.** Writing B = H + K also majorises — K is the Fejér kernel and nonnegative — but with excess 2, handing away a factor of two before the argument starts; the integral said 1.993 and that is how it was found. And **the poles must be removed analytically**: B's defining bracket has a double pole at every non-positive integer that the sin² factor cancels, and doing that cancellation in floating point costs ten digits near each one. documents.title: Selberg's bracket: L¹ deficiency exactly 1/δ, falling in the type
documents.raw_status: ** VERIFIED (numerical, pointwise to 3.2×10⁻¹⁵ at four intervals and four types)
header: **Status:** VERIFIED (numerical, pointwise to 3.2×10⁻¹⁵ at four intervals and four types)

> From B, Selberg's majorant and minorant bracket any interval's indicator at any type 2πδ, verified pointwise to 3.2×10<sup>−15</sup> at four intervals and four types. Their L¹ deficiency is **exactly 1/δ** — independent of the interval's length, and *falling* in the type rather than growing in it. That last clause is precisely what rh30 §5's three routes lack: Gershgorin, Koksma and Marcinkiewicz–Zygmund all lose *linearly* in the degree. It is why (b) looked worth taking.
- B is [Beurling's majorant](rh37-majorant-b-and-pole-free-form.md); the bracket majorises and minorises an interval's indicator at any type 2πδ.

documents.title: The annihilator bound: violated at zero of the 75 points, but loose (rms log residual 0.2484)
documents.raw_status: ** VERIFIED (numerical, a genuine bound at all 75 points)
header: **Status:** VERIFIED (numerical, a genuine bound at all 75 points)
> That suggests a mechanism with the right variable in it, and it is worth building because it half works.

> A degree-(n − 1) polynomial has n − 1 roots, and the measure is symmetric under x → −x, so p<sub>c</sub> can annihilate at most ⌊(n − 1)/2⌋ **γ-pairs**. Kill the heaviest greedily — put double roots there — and the mass that survives is an explicit upper bound on y. Crucially, the heaviest pair carries exactly 1/N<sub>eff</sub> of the mass *by the definition of N<sub>eff</sub>*, so the bound is a function of x up to the shape of the weight profile.

> Built explicitly and evaluated at all 75 points, it is a genuine bound: **violated at zero of them**. And the mass it kills is x/2 times a shape factor running from 0.500 at the sparsest up to **0.965** at the densest — so N<sub>eff</sub> really is the right normalisation for annihilable mass, and that is where the collapse variable comes from.

documents.title: Inside the regime where the collapse holds, the variable buys only 5.4% over plotting against n
documents.raw_status: ** VERIFIED (numerical, equal-count bins over the 75 points)
header: **Status:** VERIFIED (numerical, equal-count bins over the 75 points)

> rh30 bins in x at fixed edges. Comparing a second variable at the *same* edges is not a comparison, because the two differ by a factor and the bins then hold different points. Score every candidate on the same partition instead: equal-count bins over the 75 points that carry the collapse.
> Three results, and none of them is what the headline suggests.

> n/N<sub>eff</sub> gives a geometric-mean spread of **1.6123**. n/PART gives **exactly the same number**, to twelve decimals: PART/N<sub>eff</sub> never varies enough to reorder the 75 points, so the two are one variable as far as the data can tell. Whatever the collapse establishes, it does not single out N<sub>eff</sub> over the participation ratio.

documents.title: The collapse profile is F(x) = 1 − x, unbiased to seven parts in a thousand
documents.raw_status: ** VERIFIED (numerical; fitted on the 75 points, rms log residual 0.1559, median ratio 0.9931)
header: **Status:** VERIFIED (numerical; fitted on the 75 points, rms log residual 0.1559, median ratio 0.9931)

> **F(x) = 1 − x**, with a median ratio of 0.9931 — unbiased to seven parts in a thousand — and an rms log residual of 0.1559, which is about ±17%. Given that the within-bin spread is a factor of two, that is as well as any single-variable curve can be expected to do, and the first three candidates are not cleanly separated by this data.
> The profile has a name and a measured error bar — F(x) = 1 − x at ±17%, unbiased.
